findings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated `sort` interpolated into ORDER BY
findings.explanation: `sort` is an arbitrary user string (`z.string().optional()`) and is concatenated directly into the SQL text. ORDER BY cannot be parameterized, so an attacker can inject expressions (e.g. subqueries or CASE-based blind extraction, or stacked clauses) and read data across orgs or cause expensive queries. Validate with an allowlist, e.g. `z.enum(['amount','created_at','id'])`, and map to hardcoded column names in code rather than interpolating the raw input.

findings.title: Keyset pagination breaks when sorting by a non-id column
findings.explanation: The `before` cursor filters `id < $2`, but results are ordered by `amount`/`created_at`. Page 2 would skip or repeat rows because id order differs from sort order. Use a composite cursor (sort value + id) with a matching WHERE like `(amount, id) < ($x, $y)`, or restrict the semantics and document that `before` only works with the default sort. The comment `Newest first, keyset pagination on id` also becomes inaccurate.

findings.title: No sort direction control and ambiguous column names
findings.explanation: Direction is hardcoded DESC, so users can't sort ascending (e.g. smallest amount). Consider an `order=asc|desc` param. Also, an unqualified column name could become ambiguous if the query later adds joins.

findings.title: Missing tests and index consideration
findings.explanation: No tests cover sorting, invalid `sort` values (should return 400), or pagination with sort. Sorting by `amount`/`created_at` filtered by `org_id` may require indexes such as `(org_id, created_at, id)` to avoid slow sorts on large orgs.
